newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium seen deciding 15 bln bfr austerity.
newsitem.headline: Belgium seen deciding 15 bln bfr austerity.

text.p: The Belgian government is set to decide on austerity measures worth 10 to 15 billion francs at the annual spring budget review this weekend, but the exercise should be fairly painless, analysts said.
"The budget review will probably consist of some small manoeuvres in social security, maybe some increases of excise duties," said JP Morgan economist Wim Deblauwe.

In October 1996 the Belgian government agreed on a 1997 budget which aims to cut the state deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 from 3.4 percent in 1996, with an 80 billion franc austerity package consisting half of increases in indirect taxes and half of spending cuts.

Analysts expect the state coffers will have an estimated shortfall of 25 billion francs -- due to disappointing receipts and an overshoot in health spending. This should be partially compensated by lower-than-expected interest rates, which should cut debt service costs by some 10 billion francs.

A government source told Reuters that the austerity effort would be "maximum 15 billion francs, probably lower". He added that it is unlikely that the government would decide on new taxes and said the budget review would focus on spending cuts in government departments.
"It will be another painless budget effort, the structural problems will not be tackled," Petercam economist Geert Noels said.
Talks about the review are set to last all weekend and will probably continue on Monday.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene is set to present the budget review to parliament on Tuesday, when he will also present an update of his government agreement.
The update is expected to focus government policy more on the reform of the justice system, following a series of paedophile murder scandals, and on the fight against unemployment.

Although analysts generaly agree that the government will manage to cut the deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP, they regret that Dehaene has not used his powers of executive rule to push through a far-reaching reform of Belgium's social security system.

Last year, parliament granted his centre-left government the power to rule by decree, which means government measures can take immediate force of law, with parliamentary approval coming only afterwards instead of before.
For the social security reform, the executive powers expire at the end of April. For everything related to the single currency, the powers expire at the end of June.
"The government has missed its chance to overhaul the social security system," JP Morgan's Debaluwe said.
